ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The upper waveform in the figure is labeled ui and is the input signal, showing periodic rectangular pulses; the lower waveform is labeled uo and is the output signal, also showing rectangular changes. Observing one period, after ui undergoes a transition, uo is triggered to enter a pulse state opposite to its original steady state; after a definite period of time, uo automatically returns to the original stable state, and the figure does not show an additional independent reset signal. This relationship of “input trigger—output transient pulse—self-recovery after timing” also appears repeatedly in the following several periods. Reasoning: This type of circuit has only one stable state, enters a transient state after being triggered, and returns by itself to the stable state after timing ends, so it should be determined to be a monostable multivibrator.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Uses the state-transition behavior: the decisive clue is that the output leaves its normal state after a trigger and then returns by itself, which distinguishes monostable operation from bistable or astable operation.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the upper waveform labeled ui as a sequence of rectangular input pulses. planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question statement only to know that the task is to infer the circuit type from the given input and output waveforms.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: A monostable multivibrator has one stable state and one quasi-stable state. An external trigger drives it temporarily into the quasi-stable state, and after a timing interval it automatically returns to the stable state. A bistable would require another trigger to return, and an astable would oscillate without input triggering.
